$comment: Cross-runtime golden vectors for Ion's `datetime` primitive.
Consumed by all three in-repo runtimes; the three implementations must produce
byte-identical CBOR for the same instant+offset.
$wireBreaking: THIS FILE IS A WIRE-FORMAT CHANGE. Every runtime previously wrote a DIFFERENT shape and no
C#    tag 0 + RFC 3339 text, but the READER was ReadDateTimeOffset().UtcDateTime, so the
offset was parsed and then discarded. +05:30 came back as UTC.
Rust  a bare CBOR array [i64 .NET-ticks, i32 offset_minutes] — not tag 0, not text, not even
the same major type. A Rust client and a C# server could not exchange a datetime AT ALL.
TS    tag 0 + Date.toISOString() — millisecond resolution, so 100ns ticks authored in C# were
silently truncated on every round trip through a browser.
The format has no users and one of its three runtimes was already unable to interoperate, so
breaking it is strictly cheaper than keeping it.

wireFormat.container: CBOR tag 0 (standard date/time string) wrapping a definite-length text string.
wireFormat.text: RFC 3339 date-time, ALWAYS in the canonical shape YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.fffffff+HH:MM.
wireFormat.fractionalDigits: EXACTLY 7, always, even when zero. 100ns is the resolution of the most precise runtime type in play (.NET's DateTimeOffset tick). Fewer digits would lose C# precision; more would be unrepresentable in C# and would make the byte-identity rule impossible to satisfy.
wireFormat.offset: ALWAYS an explicit numeric offset, and never the 'Z' abbreviation — 'Z' and '+00:00' are the same instant but different bytes, so exactly one of them has to be canonical. Writers pick '+00:00'.
wireFormat.length: The canonical text is always exactly 33 ASCII characters, so a datetime is always 36 wire bytes: c0 78 21 <33>.
wireFormat.readerLeniency: Readers accept any valid RFC 3339 fractional precision (0..9 digits, truncating past the 7th), 'Z' as well as a numeric offset, and a lower-case 't' or a space as the date/time separator. They reject a missing tag 0, any other tag, a missing offset, and unparseable text — with a TYPED decode error, never an opaque throw.
wireFormat.tagIsRequired: Tag 0 is mandatory in BOTH directions. The general rule across Ion's tagged types is that leniency is free only when the lenient form is not already some OTHER Ion type's encoding — and a bare text string is exactly how Ion's `string` type encodes, so accepting an untagged date would make `datetime` and `string` indistinguishable in a capture. The same rule makes tag 4 mandatory for `decimal` (an untagged [exponent, mantissa] pair is an `i8[2]`) and tag 258 mandatory for `Set<T>` (an untagged array is an `Array<T>`).
wireFormat.truncationNotRounding: Fractional digits past the 7th are truncated toward zero, not rounded. Rounding .9999999xx could carry into the next second and is not reproducible across runtimes.

types.cs: System.DateTimeOffset — NOT System.DateTime; the offset is part of the value and must survive the round trip.
types.ts: IonDateTime (packages/ion.webcore.js/src/baseTypes.ts) — NOT Date, which cannot hold sub-millisecond precision.

howToConsume: encode: build the value from `unixTicks` (signed 100ns intervals since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z)
and `offsetMinutes`, write it with the runtime's datetime formatter, expect `hex`.
`iso` is the exact text that must appear inside the tag-0 string.
decode: read `hex`, re-encode it, expect `hex` back.
For each entry of `decodeOnly`: read `hex`, re-encode, expect `reencodedHex`.
For each entry of `malformed`: reading `hex` must raise the runtime's TYPED decode error.

vectors.name: epoch-utc
vectors.notes: The Unix epoch. Note the offset is written out as '+00:00', never as 'Z' — writers emit a numeric offset unconditionally so there is exactly one canonical spelling.

vectors.name: epoch-minus-one-tick
vectors.notes: One 100ns tick before the epoch. Guards the negative-unixTicks path and the floor-division every runtime needs to split a negative instant into (seconds, fraction).

vectors.name: sub-millisecond
vectors.notes: SUB-MILLISECOND GUARD. .7891234 s = 7891234 ticks. The old TypeScript writer used Date.toISOString(), which has millisecond resolution, and silently truncated this to .789 — losing 1234 ticks on every C#<->TS exchange.

vectors.name: non-utc-positive-offset
vectors.notes: NON-UTC GUARD (+05:30). Same wall-clock reading as 'sub-millisecond' but a different instant. The old C# reader was ReadDateTimeOffset().UtcDateTime, which threw the offset away, so this vector and 'sub-millisecond' decoded to two different DateTimes that both re-encoded as UTC.

vectors.name: non-utc-negative-offset
vectors.notes: -05:00 on the far side of a year boundary: the same instant is 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z. A reader that discards the offset also moves this value into the wrong calendar year locally.

vectors.name: offset-max-plus-14
vectors.notes: +14:00, the largest offset RFC 3339 / .NET / chrono all accept.

vectors.name: offset-min-minus-14
vectors.notes: -14:00, the smallest offset. .NET's DateTimeOffset rejects anything beyond +/-14:00.

vectors.name: offset-with-odd-minutes
vectors.notes: +05:45 (Nepal). Offsets are not whole hours; a runtime storing offset-as-hours would corrupt this.

vectors.name: leap-day
vectors.notes: Leap day, last tick of the day.

vectors.name: max-value
vectors.notes: DateTimeOffset.MaxValue in .NET. 7 fractional digits is exactly its resolution.

vectors.name: pre-epoch
vectors.notes: A whole-second instant before 1970. unixTicks is negative.

decodeOnly.name: reads-z-suffix
decodeOnly.notes: 'Z' is a legal RFC 3339 offset and readers accept it; writers normalise it to '+00:00'.

decodeOnly.name: reads-millisecond-precision
decodeOnly.notes: COMPATIBILITY GUARD. Exactly what the previous TypeScript release wrote (Date.toISOString() with an offset re-appended). Three fractional digits are right-padded to seven.

decodeOnly.name: reads-no-fraction
decodeOnly.notes: An absent fractional part is zero.

decodeOnly.name: reads-nanosecond-precision-truncating
decodeOnly.notes: Nine fractional digits from a nanosecond-resolution peer. Digits past the seventh are TRUNCATED, never rounded (.789123456 -> .7891234, not .7891235) — rounding could carry into the next second and is not reproducible in a fixed-width integer runtime.

malformed.name: wrong-tag
malformed.notes: Tag 1 (epoch-based date-time) is a different shape and is rejected, not silently misread.

malformed.name: missing-tag
malformed.notes: A bare RFC 3339 text string with no tag 0 is REJECTED. Tag 0 is required in both directions: an untagged text string is exactly the encoding of Ion's `string` type, so accepting it would make `datetime` and `string` indistinguishable in a capture.

malformed.name: not-a-date
malformed.notes: Unparseable text must produce the runtime's typed decode error, never an opaque throw.

malformed.name: missing-offset
malformed.notes: RFC 3339 requires an offset. A local-time-without-offset string is ambiguous and is rejected rather than being guessed as UTC.
